content: Diazinon, chemically known as O,O-diethyl-O-(2-isopropyl-6-methyl-pyrimidin-4-yl) phosphorothioate, is a liquid that ranges in color from colorless to dark brown. It is a thiophosphoric acid derivative that was first developed in 1952 by the Swiss chemical company Ciba-Geigy, which later became Novartis and subsequently Syngenta. Diazinon is a non-systemic organophosphate insecticide that was historically used to control pests such as cockroaches, silverfish, ants, and fleas in residential and non-food buildings. However, its residential uses were officially canceled in 2004, although it remains approved for certain agricultural applications. The mechanism of action of diazinon involves the inhibition of acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme critical for the proper functioning of the nervous system. This inhibition disrupts normal nerve signal transmission, ultimately leading to the death of the targeted insects. In soil, diazinon exhibits low persistence, with a half-life ranging from 2 to 6 weeks. Symptoms of diazinon poisoning in humans include weakness, headaches, chest tightness, blurred vision, nonreactive pinpoint pupils, excessive salivation, sweating, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal cramps, and slurred speech. In 1988, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) banned the use of diazinon on golf courses and sod farms due to its detrimental effects on bird populations that frequented these areas. By December 31, 2004, it became illegal in the United States to sell diazinon products for outdoor, non-agricultural purposes. However, consumers who had purchased diazinon products before this date were still permitted to use them, provided they adhered to all label instructions and safety precautions. Among cultivators of carnivorous plants, diazinon is regarded as the most effective systemic insecticide for eliminating severe infestations of aphids, mealybugs, and other sap-sucking parasites, while leaving the plants unharmed. For those unable to access diazinon, alternatives such as malathion and acephate (commonly sold as Orthene) have been reported, though they are considered less effective substitutes.
